questions.q: A query against an object with millions of records filters on a custom text field that isn't indexed and matches a large portion of the table. What is the likely result?
options: The query runs just as fast as it would on a small object
The query performs poorly because it isn't selective against an indexed field, forcing a large scan
Salesforce automatically creates an index the first time the query runs
The query is blocked entirely and returns an error
questions.explain: Without a selective filter against an indexed field, a query against a high-volume object has to examine a large portion of the table instead of using an index to narrow in on matching rows, which degrades performance as volume grows.

questions.q: A trigger issues one SOQL query inside a for-loop, once per record in the triggering batch. It worked fine with 50 test records but throws governor-limit errors in production. What's the underlying design flaw?
options: The trigger isn't bulkified — it should process the whole batch in one pass rather than querying per record
The object doesn't have enough storage allocated
The trigger needs to be converted into a Big Object
The issue is unrelated to the trigger and is caused by data skew
questions.explain: Code that issues a query or DML statement per record in a loop isn't bulkified, and will hit per-transaction governor limits once enough records pass through it at once — even though it worked correctly at small test volumes.

questions.q: What is the recommended approach for processing a large, non-trivial volume of records that would exceed what a single synchronous transaction can safely handle?
options: Increase the per-transaction governor limits through a support ticket
Always process the records through Custom Metadata Types instead of Apex
Split the job across multiple simultaneous standard (synchronous) triggers
Use asynchronous processing such as Batch Apex or Queueable Apex, which chunks large volumes into governor-limit-safe pieces
questions.explain: Asynchronous processing (Batch Apex, Queueable Apex) exists specifically to break large volumes into chunks that respect per-transaction governor limits, rather than attempting the whole job synchronously.

questions.q: A manager's role is moved in the role hierarchy on an org where the affected object has significant ownership skew. What performance consequence does this lesson associate with that kind of change?
options: None — role hierarchy changes never affect data performance
It immediately increases the org's data storage allocation
It can trigger a long-running, resource-intensive sharing recalculation across every affected record
It automatically re-indexes every custom field on the object
questions.explain: Changes to the role hierarchy, sharing rules, or ownership can trigger sharing recalculation across every affected record; on a large, skewed object this becomes a resource-intensive, potentially long-running operation.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the recurring design question an architect should ask about index strategy, automation, and sharing model, taken together?
options: Whether the design assumes small data volumes or holds up at the volume the business actually expects at scale
Whether the org is on the correct Salesforce edition
Whether every object has at least one custom field
Whether the org has enabled Field Audit Trail
questions.explain: The lesson frames performance architecture as repeatedly asking whether a given design choice (indexing, automation, sharing) assumes today's small data volume or will hold up once real, expected-at-scale volume arrives.
